encounters.cc: Gradually progressive shortness of breath over several months with orthopnea requiring extra pillows and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea with nighttime coughing fits.

lines: Gradually progressive shortness of breath over several months with orthopnea requiring extra pillows and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea with nighttime coughing fits.

The patient is a 57-year-old male with end-stage renal disease on maintenance hemodialysis and chemotherapy-induced cardiomyopathy following prior doxorubicin therapy for soft-tissue sarcoma, returning to the Cardiology clinic with progressive cardiopulmonary symptoms.
Since his Nephrology evaluation one year prior for exertional dyspnea limiting daily walks, his symptoms have gradually worsened.
He reports that he notices shortness of breath most prominently when walking the fence line after breakfast.
He has begun propping himself up with extra pillows because lying flat makes his breathing feel heavy.
He reports waking at night with sudden coughing fits that settle after he sits by the open window.
He has also noticed swelling around his ankles by evening that makes his boots tighter than usual.
His appetite is fair, but he feels more easily fatigued doing chores that never used to bother him.
He denies fever or recent upper respiratory symptoms.
He describes a vague, dull sense of chest pressure with exertion that is not sharp and does not change with breathing.
He does not recall any palpitations or episodes of fainting.
He denies recent viral illnesses, tick bites, or new rashes.
He states his weight has been fairly steady, although his belt has needed a new notch lately.
He denies orthostatic dizziness but admits to feeling slowed down.
He reports that lately dawns feel heavier and fence lines feel longer.
He now pauses twice to catch his breath before he reaches the old cottonwood.
Climbing the windmill ladder, once a warmup, has become a task he plans his day around.
Neighbors have commented that he looks puffy in the face.
He denies pleuritic pain or relief when he leans forward.
He has not had recent viral gastroenteritis or flu-like illness.
He has not been back to the hospital recently except for routine checkups.
He has had no leg pain when walking on level ground and no calf tenderness.
He denies recent prolonged travel.
After a brief rest in the clinic, he states he feels about the same and is eager to get back to the ranch before sundown.
He inquires what this might mean for his work, his cattle, and his nights under the sky.

His father died of “old age” in his late 80s, and his mother is living with osteoarthritis.
No one in his family has been told they have hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or sudden cardiac death.
He says he has cut back on alcohol over the last decade and now drinks only on holidays.
He has never used cocaine or other stimulants.
He does not smoke and has not smoked in the past.
He eats a simple diet of beans, eggs, and beef when available.
He prefers his coffee black, without milk or sugar.
But he says wife prefers her coffee with milk.
His job keeps him outdoors in all seasons.
He has lived most of his adult life on a ranch in Nevada.
The silence of the ranch he says is broken only by the lowing of cows and the steady hum of the wind sweeping across open plains.
At night, under a sky scattered with a thousand stars, he sometimes feels both small and infinite, as if the desert itself has claimed him as one of its own.
On exam today, he appears comfortable at rest but becomes winded while changing positions.
His jugular veins are mildly distended when reclining and soften when he sits up.
Lung exam reveals fine crackles at the bases that clear only partially with deep breaths.
Cardiac exam reveals a laterally displaced apical impulse and a soft, low-pitched extra sound early in diastole.
There is a holosystolic murmur best heard at the apex that radiates to the axilla.
His abdomen is soft with mild right upper quadrant fullness and no tenderness.
He has pitting edema to the mid-shins.
Peripheral pulses are intact and symmetric.
A chest image is performed and reviewed.
Transthoracic echocardiography is arranged to assess structure and function.
An electrocardiogram is obtained as part of the evaluation.
